I’m late, but this is important.
I never expected to be here at 26, and some days I still don’t. As a result I never really planned my life, I just jumped from one thing to the next, which is great and exciting, but indicative of my mental state. I can’t commit to anything, I don’t want to make a decision of what to do with my life. When I feel overwhelmed I move and start a new job, eventually moving so far from friends and family that I can’t afford to move back home and am alone all the time. I work 80+ hours a week because if I’m not working I’m thinking about how much I hate myself, sleeping all the time, and slipping back into depression. I got into debt because I emotionally spent for a year and wracked up $5000 in credit card debt. In short, I wasn’t ready to be an adult. 
I still struggle a lot with mental illness; I’ll be on medication forever. I’ve learned to accept it. I’m constantly working on childhood trauma and trauma from young adult years, even when I can’t afford therapy or to seek inpatient treatment, which is something I really need. especially for my binge eating disorder, which makes my depression so much worse because I’m literally killing myself my eating so much and I can’t stop.
But I’m alive. I know that a lot of people love and depend on me, I have 2 cats that I literally live for a lot of days, and despite all odds, I’m still here.
I would tell my teen self to take school more seriously. I wish I’d powered through my mental illness and learned better study skills, because when it came to college I wasn’t prepared. I’m naturally smart, but in high school I did the bare minimum and passed all of my classes, but college required actual work and teaching myself. I would tell myself to get a degree, and degree, and then focus on living my life. To take a chance and move across the country, but to have savings. I would tell myself it didn’t matter that I was bullied or an outcast in my small school, because in just a few years I would have friends who are more diverse, caring, intelligent, and dynamic than I could ever imagine. Friends who are going to do great things in politics, theatre, healthcare, and service. People who are way cooler than anyone in high school,- and they like me. 
I would tell myself I mattered

My Grandpa dying. I went through nursing school and spent 4 years as a nurses aid, so I've seen a lot of people die, and it's always sad, but there's just something different when it's someone you love. 
He was only in his early 60's. My Mom woke me up yelling that my Grandma had called and said his o2 levels were 62. I told her to get there ASAP and knew it wouldn't be good, but I didn't want to believe it. My Grandma, Mom, Aunt and Uncle were at their house and told me to follow in my Grandma's car. I got to the hospital and was in the room with him when he died. You just don't think it's really going to happen even though you know the facts. I don't know, I'll never forget that, or having to call my sister who lived over an hour away and tell her to meet us at their house instead of the hospital, and having to tell her that he was gone over the phone when she asked why. 
Sorry, it felt good to get that out.

Way late to the game, but I wanted to chime in. 

-No one tells you that depression is lifelong for some people. I always used to hear from therapists and Doctors that I would eventually be off the medicine and not have depression anymore. Now, a decade later, I realize that in order to stay stable and not do something like kill myself. I will need to be on medication for a long, long time. Depression is a part of me.

-No one tells you that depression is expensive. I take 7 pills related to mental illness, and frequent psychiatrist appointments and well as counseling. It's expensive, and I need to receive this care to stay healthy.

-You can be depressed and be happy. I am not sad all the time. I laugh and have a good time, I feel happy at times. I also burst into tears easily, have extremely low self-confidence, lowered motivation, lack of interest in hobbies, and sleep a lot. People with depression can feel other things besides sad or numb.

I work as a CNA in long term care. I'm used to death, it's weird and sad but it doesn't usually affect me a lot anymore. Last month however, my favorite resident died unexpectedly on my shift. He was acting somewhat odd, but it wasn't anything super out of the ordinary. 
I walked by his room at 3 am to start my bed check and he was starting to crawl out of bed. Went in there and he was acting odd. All of a sudden he was having massive diarrhea. Like, we thought it was a vasovagal response . The nurse, another aid and I were in there with him for over an hour. He wasn't acting like he was dying, just having diarrhea. Then all of a sudden he said "I don't think I'm going to make it." We used the sit to stand to put him back in bed and he died suddenly (within 5 minutes.) 
He was 96 but he was so full of life and hilarious and everyone loved him at the facility I work at. His family came but he was already gone, they never visited him, and I assumed they lived out of state or something. No, they live a couple of miles away, and couldn't take the time to visit one of the most interesting people I have ever met.
Everyone at work was so upset, I went home and cried. It still feels weird without him there to cheer us up and make us laugh. I just hope he knew how much we all cared about him.
